chapters.title: Book 9 — Odysseus declares himself and begins his story—-the Cicons, Lotophagi, and Cyclopes
paragraphs: Odysseus answered, “King Alcinous, it's a fine thing to listen to a singer with a voice as god-given as this one has. There is nothing better or more pleasant than when a whole people feast together in good order, the guests seated and listening while the tables are loaded with bread and meat, and the steward draws wine and fills every man's cup. That is as beautiful a sight as anyone could see. But now, since you want to hear the story of my sufferings, and so stir up my grief all over again, I hardly know where to begin, or how to go on and bring the tale to its end, for the gods have laid a heavy hand on me.

“First, then, let me tell you my name, so that you too may know it, and so that one day, if I survive this time of sorrow, you may become my guests, far off as I live from all of you. I am Odysseus, son of Laertes, known to all mankind for my cunning, so that my fame reaches heaven. I live in Ithaca, where there is a high mountain called Neritum, covered with forests; and not far off lie a cluster of islands close to one another—Dulichium, Same, and wooded Zacynthus. Ithaca itself lies low on the horizon, farthest out to sea toward the sunset, while the others lie apart from it toward the dawn. It is a rugged island, but it breeds brave men, and my eyes know nothing sweeter to look on. The goddess Calypso kept me with her in her cave and wanted me for a husband, and so did the cunning Circe of Aeaea; but neither of them could win me over, for nothing is dearer to a man than his own country and his parents, however fine a home he may have in a foreign land, if it is far from father and mother. But now let me tell you of the many hard adventures Zeus sent my way on my voyage home from Troy.

“When I set sail from Troy, the wind carried me first to Ismarus, the city of the Cicones. There I sacked the town and killed the men. We took their wives and a great deal of plunder, and divided it fairly among us, so that no one could complain of his share. Then I urged that we leave at once, but my men, fools that they were, would not listen, and stayed there drinking heavily and slaughtering sheep and cattle by the shore. Meanwhile the Cicones called for help from other Cicones living inland, who were more numerous, stronger, and better trained in war, skilled at fighting from chariots or on foot as the moment demanded. They came in the morning as thick as the leaves and blossoms of summer, and heaven turned against us, so that we were hard pressed. They drew up their battle line by the ships, and both sides hurled their bronze-tipped spears at one another. As long as the morning lasted and the day was still climbing, we held our ground against them, though they outnumbered us; but when the sun went down, at the hour when men unyoke their oxen, the Cicones broke us, and we lost six men from every ship. The rest of us got away.

“From there we sailed on with heavy hearts, glad to have escaped death but grieving for our lost comrades, and we did not leave until we had called out three times to each man who had died at the hands of the Cicones. Then Zeus sent the North Wind against us in a screaming gale, so that land and sky vanished in thick cloud and night rushed down out of the heavens. We let the ships run before the storm, but the wind tore our sails to rags, and we took them down for fear of wreck and rowed hard for shore. There we lay two days and two nights, worn out with toil and grief, but on the morning of the third day we raised the masts again, made sail, and took our places, leaving wind and helmsmen to steer the ships. I would have reached home safely then, had not the North Wind and the current turned against me as I rounded Cape Malea, and driven me off course, past the island of Cythera.

“From there foul winds swept me along for nine days over the sea, and on the tenth we reached the land of the Lotus-eaters, who live on a food that grows from a kind of flower. We put in there for fresh water, and my crews took their midday meal on the shore by the ships. When they had eaten and drunk, I sent two men ahead to find out what sort of people lived there, with a third to go along as herald. They set off at once and fell in with the Lotus-eaters, who meant them no harm, but gave them the lotus to eat. It was so sweet that anyone who tasted it lost all wish to bring back word or turn for home, wanting only to stay among the Lotus-eaters, munching the lotus, forgetting the way back entirely. I had to force them back to the ships, weeping the whole way, and tie them fast under the benches. Then I told the rest of the men to go aboard at once, for fear that anyone else might taste the lotus and give up wanting to go home, so they took their places and struck the grey sea with their oars.

“We sailed on from there, still in distress, until we reached the land of the lawless, savage Cyclopes. The Cyclopes neither plant nor plow; they trust to the gods and live off whatever wheat, barley, and grapes spring up wild, unplanted and untended, watered only by the rain. They have no assemblies for making laws, no councils; each one is lord over his own household, high in the mountain caves, and none of them cares anything for his neighbors.

“Now off their harbor lies a wooded, fertile island, not close to the land of the Cyclopes but not far either. Wild goats overrun it, breeding there in great numbers, undisturbed by any man, for hunters—who will suffer so much hardship in the woods and among mountain crags—never go there, and it is never plowed or grazed, but lies wild and untended year after year, home to nothing but goats. The Cyclopes have no ships, and no shipwrights to build them, so they cannot sail from place to place or cross the sea to one another's lands, as men with ships can do; if they had ships, they would have settled this island themselves, for it is a good one, and would bear anything in its season. There are meadows running down to the sea in places, well watered and thick with grass; vines would thrive there; there is flat land for plowing that would yield a heavy harvest every year, for the soil runs deep. There is a good harbor too, needing no cables or anchors, no mooring at all—a ship has only to be run onto the beach and left there until the wind turns fair for putting out to sea again. And at the head of the harbor a spring of clear water flows out from under a cave, ringed round with poplars.

“It was here that we came in, though the night was so dark that some god must have guided us, for there was nothing to be seen at all. A thick mist lay over our ships, the moon was hidden behind banks of cloud, so that no one could have made out the island even by looking for it, and no surf broke to warn us we were close to shore before we found ourselves already upon the land. Once we had beached the ships, we took down the sails, went ashore, and camped on the beach until dawn.

“When Dawn's fingers reddened the sky, we marveled at the island and wandered all over it, while the nymphs, daughters of Zeus, started the wild goats from cover so that we might have meat for our dinner. We fetched our spears and bows from the ships at once, split into three companies, and began shooting the goats. Heaven sent us fine sport: I had twelve ships with me, and each got nine goats, while my own ship's crew took ten. So we feasted through the whole long day until sunset, eating and drinking our fill, for we still had plenty of wine—each of us had filled many jars of it when we sacked the city of the Cicones, and it had not yet run out. All the while we kept our eyes on the land of the Cyclopes close by, and saw the smoke of their fires, and thought we could almost hear their voices, and the bleating of their sheep and goats. But when the sun went down and darkness came on, we lay down to sleep on the beach, and in the morning I called the men together.
“‘Stay here, the rest of you, my brave friends,’ I said, ‘while I go with my own ship's crew to find out what these people are—savages with no law among them, or a hospitable, god-fearing race.’

“I went aboard, telling my men to do the same and loose the hawsers, and they took their places and struck the grey sea with their oars. It was not far to land, and when we reached it we saw, on the face of a cliff by the sea, a great cave overhung with laurel. It was a shelter for many sheep and goats, and outside it stood a high yard walled in with stones set deep in the ground and with tall pines and oaks. This was the den of a huge creature, who was away at the time, out shepherding his flocks. He kept apart from everyone else, and lived like an outlaw, alone. He was a horror, nothing like a human being at all—more like some lone crag standing out against the sky on a high mountaintop.

“I ordered my men to draw the ship up on the beach and wait there, all but the twelve best of them, who came with me. I also brought a goatskin of the sweet dark wine that Maron, son of Euanthes, had given me—Maron the priest of Apollo, guardian god of Ismarus, who lived within the god's own wooded grounds. We had spared him when we sacked the city, along with his wife and child, out of respect for him, and in return he gave me splendid gifts: seven talents of fine gold, a bowl of silver, and twelve jars of sweet wine besides, undiluted, and so fine that no one in his house knew of it but himself, his wife, and a single housekeeper. When he drank it, he mixed twenty measures of water to one of wine, and even then the smell rising from the bowl was so wonderful that no one could resist it. I filled a great skin with this wine and brought a sack of provisions besides, for something in my heart warned me that we might meet some savage of great strength, who knew neither justice nor law.

“We soon found his cave, but he was out with his flocks, so we went inside and looked over everything. His racks groaned under cheeses, and his pens were crowded with more lambs and kids than they could properly hold, each group penned apart from the others—the older lambs, the middle ones, and the very young, all kept separate. Every pail and bowl he used for milking was swimming with whey. My men begged me to let them steal some cheeses first and get them back to the ship, then come back, drive off the lambs and kids, load them aboard, and sail away. It would have been far better if I had listened. But I would not, for I wanted to see the owner himself and see whether he would offer me a guest-gift. As it turned out, my men found him anything but welcoming.

“We lit a fire, offered some of the cheeses in sacrifice, ate some ourselves, and sat waiting for him to come in with his flocks. When he arrived, he was carrying a huge load of dry wood to burn for his supper, and he flung it down on the floor of the cave with such a crash that we scrambled in terror to the back of the cavern. He drove all his ewes inside, along with the she-goats he meant to milk, leaving the males, rams and billy-goats, out in the yard. Then he rolled a huge stone across the mouth of the cave—so huge that twenty-two heavy four-wheeled wagons could not have dragged it from where it stood against the doorway. That done, he sat down and milked his ewes and goats in turn, and set each one's young beside her. Half the milk he curdled and set aside in wicker baskets, and the rest he poured into bowls to drink with his supper. When he had finished all his work, he lit the fire—and then he caught sight of us, and said:
“‘Strangers—who are you? Where do you sail from? Are you traders, or do you roam the sea like raiders, ready to risk your own lives and bring death to others?’

“His huge voice and monstrous shape terrified us, but I managed to answer: ‘We are Achaeans, on our way home from Troy, but the will of Zeus and hard weather have driven us far off our course. We are men of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, whose fame has spread across the whole world, for he sacked a great city and killed so many men there. We come to you as suppliants, hoping you will show us some hospitality, or at least give us the gifts a guest may rightly expect. Fear the anger of the gods, my lord—we are your suppliants, and Zeus watches over travelers and strangers, and avenges any wrong done to them.’

“He gave me a pitiless answer. ‘Stranger,’ he said, ‘you are a fool, or else a stranger to this country, to speak to me of fearing the gods or their anger. We Cyclopes care nothing for Zeus or any of your blessed gods, for we are far stronger than they are. I will spare neither you nor your men out of any regard for Zeus, unless I myself am in the mood for it. Now tell me—where did you leave your ship when you came ashore? Was it round the point, or does it lie straight off the land?’

“He asked this to draw me out, but I was too cunning to be caught that way, and answered with a lie. ‘Poseidon,’ I said, ‘wrecked my ship on the rocks at the far end of your country, driving us onto them from the open sea. I and these men with me are the only ones who escaped.’

“The brute answered not a word, but sprang up, seized two of my men at once, and dashed them to the ground like puppies. Their brains spilled out on the floor and soaked the earth with blood. Then he tore them limb from limb and made his meal of them, gulping down flesh, bones, marrow, and entrails alike, like a lion in the wilderness, leaving nothing. We wept and raised our hands to heaven at the horror of it, not knowing what else to do; and when the Cyclops had filled his great belly with human flesh and washed it down with a drink of unmixed milk, he stretched out among his sheep and fell asleep. I thought at first of drawing my sword and driving it into his chest as he slept, but I held back, knowing that if I did, we would all die there with him, for none of us could have moved the huge stone he had set across the doorway. So we stayed where we were, groaning and weeping, until morning came.

“When Dawn's fingers reddened the sky again, he lit his fire, milked his ewes and goats in their turn, and set each one's young beside her; and when his work was done, he seized two more of my men and made his morning meal of them. Then, with ease, he rolled the stone from the door, drove his flocks out, and put it back in place again just as easily as a man setting a lid on a quiver. Then he shouted and whistled his sheep on up the mountain, and I was left to think of some way to take revenge and win myself glory.

“In the end I judged this the best plan. The Cyclops had a great club lying near one of the sheepfolds—green olive wood, cut and left to season so he could use it as a staff once it dried. It was so huge we could only compare it to the mast of a twenty-oared trading ship, broad enough to cross the open sea. I went up to it and cut off about six feet, then handed the piece to my men and told them to smooth one end evenly, which they did, and I finished sharpening that same end to a point myself and hardened it in the fire. Then I hid it under the heaps of dung that lay everywhere about the cave, and told the men to draw lots for which four of them would help me lift it and twist it into the monster's eye while he slept. The lot fell on exactly the men I would have chosen myself, and I made the fifth. That evening the wretch came back from his shepherding and drove his whole flock into the cave, this time leaving none outside in the yard—whether by some whim of his own or because a god prompted him, I cannot say. Once he had set the stone back across the doorway, he sat down, milked his ewes and goats in their turn, set each one's young beside her, and when his work was finished, he seized two more of my men and made his supper of them. So I came up to him, holding out a wooden bowl of the dark wine.

“‘Here, Cyclops,’ I said, ‘you've had a great deal of human flesh—now drink some wine, to see what sort of drink we carried in our ship. I brought it as an offering for you, hoping you might take pity on me and send me on my way home. But you rage on so, no one could bear it. You should be ashamed of yourself. How do you expect anyone to visit you again, when you treat your guests like this?’

“He took the bowl and drank it down, and was so delighted with the taste that he begged for another. ‘Give me more, if you please,’ he said, ‘and tell me your name at once, so I can give you a guest-gift that will please you. We have wine too in this country, from grapes our own soil grows and our own sun ripens, but this is nectar and ambrosia poured into one.’

“So I gave him more. Three times I filled the bowl for him, and three times he drained it without a thought. Then, when I saw the wine had gone to his head, I spoke to him as smoothly as I could. ‘Cyclops, you ask my name—I will tell it to you, and you shall give me the guest-gift you promised. My name is Nobody. That is what my father and mother and all my friends have always called me.’
“And the brute answered, ‘Then I will eat Nobody last, after all his comrades, and eat his comrades first. That will be my gift to him.’

“As he spoke he reeled and fell backward, sprawled on the ground, and a deep sleep took hold of him. His head lolled back over his great neck. Soon he began to retch, bringing up wine and gobbets of human flesh together, for he was very drunk. Then I thrust the stake deep into the embers to heat it, and spoke to my men to keep their courage up, in case any of them lost heart. When the wood, green as it was, was just about to catch fire and glow, I drew it from the flames, and my men gathered round me, for some god had filled their hearts with courage. We drove the sharpened point into the monster's eye, and I leaned my whole weight on it and twisted it round and round, the way a man bores a hole in a ship's timber with an auger, which two men can keep turning as long as they like with a wheel and strap. So we turned the red-hot stake in his eye, until the blood boiled up around it, and the steam from the scorching eyeball singed his brow and lashes, and the roots of the eye crackled in the fire. As a blacksmith plunges a red-hot axe or adze into cold water to temper it—for that is what gives strength to iron—and it hisses loudly as he does, so his eye hissed around the olive stake. He gave a terrible scream, and the cave rang with it. We ran back in terror, but he wrenched the stake, dripping with blood, out of his eye and hurled it from him, howling in a frenzy of pain, and calling out to the other Cyclopes who lived scattered on the windswept heights nearby. They heard him and came from every side, gathering round the cave to ask what was wrong with him.

“‘What ails you, Polyphemus,’ they called, ‘crying out like this in the peaceful night, and keeping the rest of us from sleep? Is someone driving off your sheep? Is someone trying to kill you, by force or by treachery?’
“And Polyphemus called back to them from inside the cave, ‘Nobody is killing me by treachery; nobody is killing me by force.’
“‘Well then,’ they said, ‘if nobody is attacking you, you must be sick. Sickness comes from Zeus, and there's no help for that—you had better pray to your father Poseidon.’

“So they went away, and I laughed to myself at how well my trick had worked. But the Cyclops, groaning in his agony, felt about with his hands until he found the stone and pulled it from the doorway. Then he sat in the opening with his arms stretched wide, ready to catch anyone who tried to slip out among the sheep—thinking, I suppose, that I might be foolish enough to try it.

“For my part, I kept turning over in my mind how I might save my own life and my men's, for the danger was great, and I racked my brains as any man does when his life hangs on it. In the end, this seemed to me the best plan. The rams were well grown, with heavy dark fleeces, so I bound them quietly together in threes with the willow withies—cords the monster used for his own bed. The man in the middle of each three would be hidden, with a ram to either side to cover him, so that three sheep carried one man. As for myself, there was one ram finer than all the rest, and I got a grip on his back, curled myself up under his shaggy belly, and hung on there, face upward, gripping his fleece tightly and not letting go.

“So we waited, sick with fear, until morning came. When Dawn's fingers reddened the sky, the rams hurried out to graze, while the ewes stood bleating round the pens, still unmilked, their udders swollen and heavy. Their master, for all his pain, felt along the back of each sheep as it went out, but never thought to feel underneath, where the men were hidden. Last of all came the ram, weighed down by his own thick fleece and by me clinging beneath him. Polyphemus took hold of him and said:

“‘My good ram, why are you the last out of the cave this morning? You've never lagged behind the ewes before—you're always first, striding out to the flowering meadow or the bubbling spring, first out and first home again at night. But now you're last of all. Is it because you know your master has lost his eye—blinded by that wretched Nobody and his crew, who got me down while I was drunk? He has not got away yet, I promise you. If only you could talk and tell me where he's hiding, I would dash his brains out on the ground until they were scattered all over this cave, and get some satisfaction for what that good-for-nothing Nobody has done to me.’

“So saying, he drove the ram outside. When we had gone a little way from the cave and the yard, I slipped out first from under the ram's belly, then freed my men. As for the sheep—fine, fat animals—we kept them moving in the right direction and drove them all the way down to the ship. Our crew rejoiced to see us alive, but wept for the men we had lost. I made signs to them, nodding and frowning, to hush their crying, and told them to load the sheep aboard at once and put out to sea. So they went aboard, took their places, and struck the grey sea with their oars. And when I had gone as far out as my voice could carry, I began to taunt the Cyclops.

“‘Cyclops,’ I called, ‘you should have taken a better measure of the man whose comrades you meant to eat in your cave. Your crimes were bound to catch up with you—you dared to eat your own guests in your own house, and now Zeus and the other gods have paid you back.’

“This drove him into a greater fury than ever. He tore the peak off a high mountain and hurled it at us; it fell just short of the ship's bow, missing the steering-oar by a hair. The sea heaved up where the rock struck, and the wave it raised drove us back toward the shore, forcing the ship almost onto the mainland again. But I snatched up a long pole and shoved us off, motioning to my men with a nod of my head to row for their lives, and they bent to it with a will. When we had put twice the distance between us, I was ready to taunt the Cyclops again, but my men begged me to hold my tongue.

“‘Don't provoke this savage any further,’ they begged. ‘He has already thrown one rock that drove us back to the mainland, and we were sure it meant the death of us. If he had heard even one more sound from us just then, he would have smashed our heads and the ship's timbers to splinters with the next jagged rock he hurled—he can throw them a long way.’

“But I would not listen, and shouted back at him in my fury: ‘Cyclops, if anyone ever asks who blinded you and ruined your looks for good, tell them it was the valiant warrior Odysseus, son of Laertes, who lives in Ithaca.’

“At that he groaned aloud and cried, ‘So the old prophecy is coming true at last! There was a prophet here once, a big, powerful man named Telemus, son of Eurymus, the best seer among us, who grew old prophesying for the Cyclopes. He told me all this would happen to me one day—that I would lose my sight at the hands of Odysseus. But I always pictured some huge and mighty hero coming against me, not this—this puny little weakling, who got the better of me with wine and caught me off guard. Come back, Odysseus, and let me give you the gifts a guest deserves, and let me beg Poseidon to speed you on your way—for Poseidon is my father, and he alone, if he wishes, can heal me. No other god or man can do it.’
“I called back, ‘I only wish I could be as sure of killing you outright and sending you down to the house of Hades, as I am that not even Poseidon will ever heal that eye of yours.’

“At this he lifted his hands to the starry sky and prayed: ‘Hear me, great Poseidon—if I am truly your own son, grant that Odysseus may never reach his home alive. But if he must get back to his friends at last, let him come late, and badly, having lost all his companions, in a ship that is not his own—and let him find trouble waiting for him in his house.’

“So he prayed, and Poseidon heard him. Then he picked up a rock, far bigger than the first, swung it up, and hurled it with tremendous force. It fell just short of the ship, missing the steering-oar by a hair once more. The sea heaved where it struck, and the wave carried us onward, driving us toward the shore of the island.

“At last we reached the island where we had left the rest of our ships, and found our comrades there, grieving for us and watching anxiously for our return. We ran the ship up onto the sand and climbed out onto the beach; then we brought the Cyclops's sheep ashore too, and divided them fairly among us, so that no one had cause to complain. But my men agreed I should have the ram for my own share, over and above the rest, and I sacrificed him there on the shore and burned his thighbones to Zeus, lord of all. But Zeus paid no heed to my offering; already he was planning how he might destroy all my ships and every man who sailed with me.

“So we feasted the whole day long, until the sun went down, on meat and sweet wine; and when the light failed and darkness came on, we lay down to sleep on the beach. When Dawn's fingers reddened the sky again, I roused the men and told them to go aboard and loose the hawsers. They took their places and struck the grey sea with their oars, and we sailed on, glad to have escaped death, but grieving still for the friends we had lost.”
